name: MOTS-c
alsoCalled: Mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c
evidenceNote: The metabolic and exercise benefits come from mouse studies. In people, there are only observational measurements of the body's own MOTS-c and one four-week trial of a modified analog in 20 adults; MOTS-c itself has no published human treatment data.
summary: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that improved metabolism in mice. Untested as a treatment in people and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: MOTS-c is a short peptide made from instructions in the DNA of mitochondria, the cell's energy units. In mice it improved insulin sensitivity, prevented diet-induced weight gain, and extended running capacity in old age. In people, exercise raises the body's own MOTS-c, but no published trial has given MOTS-c itself to humans. It is not FDA-approved. Since October 2026, an interim HHS policy lets 503A pharmacies compound it without enforcement action, which is not an approval. WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded not in the main genome in the cell nucleus but in the separate, much smaller set of DNA carried by mitochondria [1][2]. Its name describes where the code sits: a short open reading frame inside the gene for the mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA [1].

It was described in 2015 by a team that included Pinchas Cohen, as part of a small family of mitochondrial-derived peptides that also includes humanin [1]. Levels of MOTS-c circulate in the blood and appear to fall with age, which drew interest from longevity researchers [2].

Synthetic MOTS-c is now sold online as an injectable research peptide, often marketed for fat loss, endurance, and healthy aging. Those claims run ahead of the evidence, which in people is close to nonexistent.

The original study found that MOTS-c acts mainly on skeletal muscle. Inside muscle cells it blocks the folate cycle, which slows the production of purines (building blocks of DNA). The resulting change in cell chemistry switches on AMPK, an enzyme that senses low energy and pushes cells to take up glucose and burn fuel [1].

Under metabolic stress, MOTS-c can also move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and change which nuclear genes are switched on, including genes involved in metabolism and protein quality control [2][4]. That makes it an unusual case of the mitochondria sending instructions back to the nucleus.

Exercise appears to be one natural trigger. In human volunteers, a hard bout of exercise raised MOTS-c in muscle and in the blood, which is why researchers have proposed it as an exercise-sensitive signal [3][4]. Whether regular training changes MOTS-c over the long run is less clear, and studies disagree [3].

No. MOTS-c is not approved for any use. On its compounding safety page, the FDA lists it among bulk peptides whose nominations were withdrawn, and states it had found no human exposure data for MOTS-c by any route and lacked key information on whether it could cause harm [6]. The agency also flagged a possible risk of immune reactions and difficulties in characterizing peptide impurities [6].

That position shifted in late October 2026. After an FDA advisory committee voted in July to back adding six peptides to the 503A bulks list, HHS announced an interim policy under which it will not take enforcement action against 503A compounding pharmacies that make products from MOTS-c, BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, semax, or TB-500 [10][7][8]. FDA's own scientific staff had recommended against adding these peptides [11][8].

The policy is not an approval and does not establish that MOTS-c is safe or effective [10][8]. It requires a patient-specific prescription and quality-tested ingredients, has no fixed end date, and can be revisited if a safety signal appears [10][8]. For athletes, WADA lists MOTS-c as a prohibited metabolic modulator, banned in and out of competition [5].

blocks.text: Most of what is known comes from mice. Injected MOTS-c prevented both the insulin resistance that comes with aging and the weight gain that comes with a high-fat diet [1]. A later study found it improved running performance in young, middle-aged, and old mice, and that treatment started late in life, three times a week, increased physical capacity [4].

rows: Prevented diet-induced obesity and age-related insulin resistance [1]
Better physical performance at all ages tested, including late-life treatment [4]
Natural MOTS-c rose in muscle and blood after hard exercise [3][4]
20 adults with obesity and fatty liver
Liver enzymes and glucose fell versus placebo; liver fat fell similarly in both groups [9]

blocks.text: The only controlled human dosing data come from CB4211, a modified version of MOTS-c developed by CohBar, a company founded by Cohen [9]. In a four-week placebo-controlled study of 20 adults with obesity and fatty liver, it lowered the liver enzyme ALT by about 21% from baseline against 4% on placebo, and glucose by 6% [9]. Liver fat fell by almost the same amount on placebo, body weight showed only a trend, and the results came from a company press release rather than a peer-reviewed paper [9].

CB4211 is not the same molecule as the MOTS-c sold online, so even these small results do not transfer directly. A 2023 review noted that no effective way to use MOTS-c in the clinic had yet been developed [2]. No human study has tested the endurance, fat loss, or anti-aging effects seen in mice.
